structure.title: Chapters I–III · A tenant visits his landlord
structure.text: Lockwood arrives at Wuthering Heights confident he can identify a wife, a servant and the master of a house by looking round a room. He gets almost every relationship wrong. Snow forces him to spend the night with names scratched into a window ledge and a good deal of explaining still to come.

structure.title: Chapters IV–XVII · Nelly tells the children's history
structure.text: Back at the Grange, the housekeeper begins with a child brought home from Liverpool. Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw form an alliance within a household whose authority can pass overnight to the person who hates them. A visit to the neighbouring Lintons introduces another household's standards of beauty, manners and marriage.

structure.title: Chapters XVIII–XXXIV · The next children inherit the houses
structure.text: The same few names begin to recur among a second generation. The people receiving the children, deciding whom they may visit and controlling their education can remember exactly where their own injuries were sustained. Crossing the short distance between the two houses acquires consequences all over again.

people.name: Heathcliff
people.role: Child taken into the Earnshaw household
people.text: Old Earnshaw can give the boy shelter and preference without giving him a secure legal position or an account of his origins. Heathcliff grows up knowing precisely how much of a child's everyday life can depend on the private likes of the person who owns the house.

people.name: Catherine Earnshaw
people.text: She knows the ease of running wild with Heathcliff and the pleasures of being welcomed as a lady at the Grange. When she tries to explain what both futures mean to her, who happens to overhear which part of the explanation becomes desperately important.

people.name: Nelly Dean and Lockwood
people.text: Nelly has washed, nursed, carried messages and sometimes refused to carry them. She knows much that an outsider could never discover. Lockwood puts that knowledge into his own written account, despite the social misjudgments we have already watched him make.

context.title: Two houses and repeated names
context.text: Wuthering Heights belongs to the Earnshaw story, Thrushcross Grange to the Lintons. Marriages carry names and claims between them. A child can bear the surname of a family whose house is entirely strange to her, a difficulty Lockwood shares with a first-time reader.

notice.text: Attend to the moments Nelly leaves a room.
notice.why: She may hear the beginning of a conversation, miss its end and supply an interpretation years later. At other times she is the person who opens a door or delays a letter. Her account includes decisions she made herself.

notice.text: Follow who can read a name or a letter.
notice.why: A carved word can summon a history. An unopened or inaccessible letter can keep two people apart. Denying a child the chance to learn to read is one way the adults can extend the life of a quarrel.

passages.quote: it was covered with writing scratched on the paint

opening: Heathcliff arrives at a Yorkshire farmhouse as a child nobody there knows what to do with. Catherine becomes his closest companion; her brother makes sure he understands his inferior place. The attachment growing between them absorbs the injuries around it, until love and the desire to hurt become dangerously entangled. Emily Brontë follows what happens when people refuse to let a grievance end with them, across houses, marriages, and children who inherit arrangements made long before they had any chance to object.
